article.title: How to Test Hair Porosity at Home: 3 Simple Methods
article.meta_description: Learn how to test hair porosity at home with the float, slip-and-slide and spray tests, plus how to read your results and style around them well.
article.h1: How to Test Hair Porosity at Home (and What to Do With the Result)
article.body_html:
To test hair porosity at home, start with clean, product-free hair and try two or three simple checks: the float test, the slip-and-slide strand test and the spray bottle test. Compare the results to see whether your hair tends toward low, medium or high porosity. These tests are rough guides, not lab measurements, so treat the outcome as a starting point for choosing products and styling habits.

What hair porosity is (and what it isn't)

Porosity describes how readily your hair takes in and holds onto moisture. Each strand is covered in overlapping scales called the cuticle. When the cuticle lies flat and tight, water and products tend to enter slowly. When it is raised or uneven, they tend to enter quickly and may leave just as fast.

Porosity vs. hair type, strand width and density

Porosity is not the same as hair type. Your type (straight, wavy, curly or coily) describes the shape of the strand and the curl pattern. Strand width is how thick each hair is, and density is how many hairs you have. Two people with identical curl patterns can have very different porosity. If you are not sure of your type yet, take the hair type quiz first, then come back here.

Why people want to know it

The practical reason is product choice and routine: how heavy a cream to use, how to apply it, and how much heat feels right. It is a styling characteristic. It is not a measure of whether your hair or scalp is healthy.

Prep first: how to get a fair result

Most inaccurate results come from skipping preparation. Product residue can make hair repel water, and oils can make it float, which skews almost every test.

Start with clean hair free of oils, conditioner and styling products

Wash with a clarifying or regular shampoo, rinse well, and let your hair dry completely without applying conditioner, oil, leave-in or gel. Wait until the next day if you can, so you are testing your hair and not your products.

Collect strands from different areas

Use a few strands that have shed naturally, for example from your brush, and pull them from different areas if possible. The hair near your crown, your nape and the ends of your lengths can behave differently, especially if you have colored or heat-styled parts of your hair.

Test more than once and use more than one method

One test is a snapshot. Running two or three methods, and repeating one of them on another day, gives you a more reliable picture than any single result.

Test 1: The float test (treat it with caution)

Step-by-step method

  1. Fill a clear glass with room-temperature water.
  2. Drop in two or three clean, dry strands.
  3. Watch for a few minutes without stirring or touching the glass.
  4. Note whether the strands float, hover in the middle or sink to the bottom.

How people usually read the result

Strands that stay at the top are often read as lower porosity. Strands that sink quickly are often read as higher porosity. Strands that hover in the middle are often read as medium.

Why it can mislead

The float test is popular but far from definitive. Leftover product, natural oils, the weight of a single strand, the surface tension of the water and how long you wait can all change the outcome. A strand that looks like it floats may simply be coated in residue. Use this test as one clue among several.

Test 2: The slip-and-slide strand test

Step-by-step method

  1. Take a clean, dry strand and hold it firmly by one end, near the root end.
  2. With your other thumb and forefinger, slide up the strand toward the root.
  3. Notice whether your fingers glide smoothly or catch on bumps and roughness.

What the feel generally suggests

A smooth glide is often associated with a tighter, flatter cuticle, which tends to go with lower porosity. A bumpy or rough feel is often associated with a more raised cuticle, which tends to go with higher porosity.

Limits

Roughness can also come from product buildup, heat styling, chemical processing or simply the natural texture of your hair. Because the result is based on feel, it is also subjective, so compare it with another test before drawing conclusions.

Test 3: The spray bottle or water absorption test

Step-by-step method

  1. Start with clean, fully dry hair and no products.
  2. Section off a small piece of hair and lightly spritz it with plain water.
  3. Watch what the water does over the next minute or two.

What the result tends to suggest

If water beads up on the surface and sits there before soaking in, your hair may lean toward lower porosity. If the hair soaks up water almost instantly and feels wet through quickly, it may lean toward higher porosity. A gradual, even absorption sits in the middle.

Why it works best on freshly clean hair

Any coating on the hair can make water bead up, so this test is only meaningful on freshly cleansed strands. Try it on a few different sections of your head, since the ends often absorb differently from the roots.

Reading your results: low, medium or high porosity

What you might notice

ObservationOften points to low porosityOften points to medium porosityOften points to high porosity
Float testStrand stays on topStrand hovers in the middleStrand sinks fast
Slip-and-slideFeels smoothMostly smooth, slight textureFeels bumpy or rough
Spray bottleWater beads on the hairAbsorbs steadilySoaks in right away
Everyday behaviorSlow to get wet, slow to dry, products can sit on topModerate drying time, usually holds stylesWets and dries fast, tends toward frizz, products seem to vanish

What to do if your tests disagree

This is common. Give more weight to how your hair behaves day to day: how long it takes to dry, whether products sit on top or disappear, and how it handles humidity. If the tests still conflict, you may have a mix, such as a smoother root area and rougher, more processed ends.

Porosity differs across your head and changes over time

Coloring, bleaching, heat styling, sun, weather and even rough brushing can all shift how your hair behaves. Older, more processed lengths often differ from newer growth near the scalp. Retest every few months, or after a big change like a new color, and treat each result as a snapshot.

What to do with your result: general styling guidance

This is cosmetic routine guidance only, not treatment. Adjust it to what you see in your own hair.

Low porosity

  • Choose lightweight products such as lotions, mousses and light gels over thick butters and heavy oils.
  • Apply products to damp hair, and gentle warmth, such as a warm towel, can help products spread.
  • Avoid layering many products, which can leave hair feeling coated or weighed down.

Medium porosity

  • This type is usually flexible, so a simple routine of a cleanser, a conditioner and a styler often works.
  • Keep an eye on changes after coloring or frequent heat.

High porosity

  • Try richer creams and butters, and consider sealing with an oil or butter after a water-based product to help it last.
  • Use lower heat settings and a heat protectant, and keep brushing gentle.
  • Apply products generously on soaking-wet hair, since it tends to dry quickly.

What these tests can't tell you

They don't assess hair or scalp health

Porosity tests describe how your strands take in water. They do not evaluate your hair's health, and nothing in this article is medical advice. AI feedback of any kind, including from apps, is not medical advice either. If you have any concern about your hair or scalp, see a dermatologist or doctor.

When to get professional advice

Talk to a doctor or dermatologist if you notice a sudden change in texture, unusual shedding, scalp pain, irritation or patches. A porosity test cannot explain those changes.

From porosity to a look you love

Once you know how your hair behaves, use that to choose a style that suits it. Pair your porosity result with your curl pattern from the hair type quiz, then work through a five-step way to choose a haircut that suits your texture and face shape. Low porosity hair that dries slowly may suit a style that needs less daily product. Higher porosity hair that frizzes in humidity may suit a cut that works with air-drying. When you have a shortlist, you can preview hairstyles on your face before committing.

How FitCheck AI can help with your hair look

To be clear, FitCheck AI does not measure porosity, assess hair health or detect any hair or scalp condition. What it can help with is the next step: turning what you know about your hair into a look. You can explore hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, and use live hair analysis with your camera for cosmetic hairstyle and color ideas. You can also try different hairstyles on your own face, as the app generates AI images of you from your photo. Treat these as a visual starting point and a second opinion, not a professional stylist's advice.

faqs.question: Is the float test accurate?
faqs.answer: It is a rough indicator at best. Product residue, natural oils, strand weight and how long you wait can all change the result, so a floating strand does not guarantee low porosity. Combine it with the slip-and-slide or spray bottle test and pay attention to how your hair behaves in daily life.

faqs.question: How often should I retest my hair porosity?
faqs.answer: Every few months is plenty for most people. Retest sooner after coloring, bleaching, a big change in heat styling or a major change in climate, since these can shift how your hair absorbs water. Always test on clean, product-free hair so the results are comparable.

faqs.question: Can coloring, bleaching or heat change my porosity?
faqs.answer: They often can. Chemical processing and frequent high heat tend to make the cuticle rougher, so processed hair commonly behaves more like higher porosity hair than untouched hair does. This is why the ends of your hair may test differently from the roots.

faqs.question: Is porosity the same as curl pattern or hair type?
faqs.answer: No. Hair type describes strand shape and curl pattern, while porosity describes how readily the strand absorbs and holds moisture. Strand width and density are separate again. Two people with the same curl pattern can have different porosity.

faqs.question: Can the FitCheck AI app test my hair porosity?
faqs.answer: No, the app does not measure porosity or assess hair health. It offers hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, live hair analysis for cosmetic style ideas, and AI previews of hairstyles on your own photo. Its feedback is not medical advice, so see a dermatologist or doctor about any hair or scalp concern.

factual_issues: Test 2 (slip-and-slide) gives contradictory instructions. It says to hold the strand "by one end, near the root end" and then to "slide up the strand toward the root." If you hold the root end, you cannot slide toward it. The standard method is to hold the strand by the tip end (or the strand's middle) and run your fingers up toward the root against the cuticle. As written, a reader cannot do the test correctly, so this step must be rewritten.
review.notes: The article matches the informational intent well. It covers prep, three at-home methods with caveats, a results table, advice for when tests disagree, styling guidance by porosity level, and clear limits. It stays honest that these tests are rough guides. The app section is accurate and appropriately restrained: it states that the app does not measure porosity or assess hair health, and it only mentions features listed in APP_FACTS (hairstyle inspiration, live cosmetic hair analysis, AI hairstyle try-on from a photo, Android free, iOS coming soon). There are no invented statistics, studies or testimonials, and no medical claims. Fix the slip-and-slide step, then it should pass. Minor, non-blocking: "Most inaccurate results come from skipping preparation" is an unsourced generalization and could be softened to "Many". The high-porosity advice to apply products on soaking-wet hair could be phrased as optional. Sealing with oil is presented as a general styling tip, which is fine.
